title: Tech for Change Community Project: Smart Beehive
intro: Year 7 and Year 8 are working together on one community project. Open this lesson’s topic and prepare your team’s Trello card here.

topics.title: What problem are we trying to solve?
learn: Think about who might need help and what might be difficult. Your question will guide your research in Lesson 2.
An observation is a detail you can point to in a photo. An assumption is an explanation you haven’t checked yet.
steps: Look at each photo. Write one detail you can point to in each.
Choose bees, a beekeeper or both. Write one possible difficulty. Mark what you are still guessing.
On your team card, write one question for Lesson 2, who will investigate it and the due date.
topics.result: Your team has observations from the photos, a possible problem and one question for Lesson 2.
cardChecklist: One detail you can point to in each photo.
Who might need help, one possible difficulty and what is still a guess.
One question for Lesson 2, who will investigate it and when it’s due.
topics.teacherQuestion: If you see a brick on the lid, what can you point to? What are you guessing about its job?
topics.teacherWatch: Model: “I can see a brick on the lid” is an observation. “It might keep the lid from moving” is an assumption. Ask what evidence could check that explanation. Save solution ideas for later.

topics.title: Research a real DIY build
learn: Find a documented DIY hive or hive-monitoring build. Look at parts, materials, dimensions and access, not just the sensor.
Record the source and units. Separate reported dimensions from your own ideas. If a size is missing, ask; do not invent it or use an AI guess.
steps: Choose one actual build with photos, plans or a parts list. Save its source link.
Record one useful finding about a part, material or stated dimension. Link it to the question you wrote in Lesson 1.
Add one unanswered question and a next task to your team card. Include an owner and due date.
topics.result: A source-backed physical-design finding and a clear next research question.
cardChecklist: Source link and what the build is for.
One supported finding about a part, material or dimension, with units where needed.
One limitation or missing detail, plus the next task, owner and due date.
topics.teacherQuestion: What does the source actually show? Which size or material choice still needs evidence?
topics.teacherWatch: Check that the source supports the finding. Research informs a classroom prototype; it does not prove bee health or justify unapproved work on a real hive.

topics.title: Brainstorm and compare ideas
learn: Imagine more than one response to the problem. A simple housing or access change may be useful alongside an electronic idea.
Compare ideas using the need and your evidence. A labelled sketch can show parts, position and access; it need not be a polished drawing.
steps: Make two different ideas for your problem. Sketch and label each one.
Compare how each could help, what evidence supports it and what still needs testing.
Choose a provisional direction. Add one small next test to your team card with an owner and due date.
topics.result: Two compared ideas, an evidence-based provisional choice and a next test.
topics.cardTitle: Two ideas and our next test
cardChecklist: Two labelled ideas linked to our problem.
One evidence-backed reason for the provisional choice and one limitation.
The next small test, its owner and due date.
topics.teacherQuestion: How are the two ideas different? What test could change your choice?
topics.teacherWatch: Reward evidence and alternatives, not complexity. Keep missing dimensions as questions until researched; do not present an untested design as field-ready.

topics.title: Plan a small prototype
learn: Choose one idea that answers your problem. Use researched constraints to plan parts, materials, access and a simple cost estimate.
Use a labelled sketch. Cite copied dimensions; label your own model dimensions as planned. Follow a verified plan for real hive sizes rather than inventing them.
steps: Choose one idea and link it to your problem and research.
Draw the smallest useful model. List materials, sourced or planned sizes and estimated costs.
Add three checks for the model, then assign the next making task and due date.
topics.result: A feasible model plan with a sketch, materials, estimated costs and three checks.
cardChecklist: Chosen idea and its link to the problem and evidence.
Labelled sketch, materials, dimensions with their source or planned status, and estimated costs.
Three checks and the next making task with an owner and due date.
topics.teacherQuestion: What is the smallest model that can answer your question? Which constraint comes from research?
topics.teacherWatch: Keep scope achievable. Separate cited hive dimensions from classroom-model choices and estimates; do not treat an AI suggestion as a verified plan.

topics.title: Make a small model
learn: Build a small digital or cardboard prototype from your plan. A model can test a useful idea without a real hive or live bees.
Keep evidence of the process: one before photo or screenshot, one change and one after image. Explain what the model can and cannot show.
steps: Check the plan and gather the approved materials or digital tools.
Make the smallest working part. Save a before photo or screenshot.
Improve one detail, save an after image and note the next test on your card.
topics.result: A small prototype with before-and-after evidence and a test to run next.
cardChecklist: Photo or screenshot of the first version.
One explained change and an after image.
What the model demonstrates, one limit and the next test with an owner and due date.
topics.teacherQuestion: Which part of the problem can this model help you test? What would it not prove?
topics.teacherWatch: Use approved classroom materials and tools. No live bees or real-hive intervention; digital simulations and cardboard models must be labelled honestly.

topics.title: Test and improve with evidence
learn: Run the three checks from your plan. Record what you expected and what actually happened, including failures.
Use the results to choose one improvement. Repeat the relevant check and explain the difference. A successful model is evidence about the model, not proof of bee health.
steps: Run three planned checks, such as fit or access, function or clarity, and repeated use. Record results.
Change one important detail and repeat the affected check. Keep both results.
Summarise what works, one remaining limit and the next task after the review.
topics.result: Three test results, an evidence-led improvement and a clear next step.
cardChecklist: Three checks with expected and actual results.
One change with before-and-after test evidence.
What works, one limitation and the next task with an owner and due date.
topics.teacherQuestion: Which result supports your claim? Did the change improve the same test?
topics.teacherWatch: Keep failures visible. Check claims against actual results and preserve the original evidence. Do not describe a classroom model as ready for real-hive use.
